1002.title: Why keep saints' days
1002.hook: remembering holy people on their day, as families remember birthdays
1002.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches mark saints' days in their calendars, with readings, prayers and sometimes feasts; some other Protestant churches honor faithful Christians of the past in sermons and stories without a calendar of saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, witnesses: Joshua to Lagos, a cloud of witnesses. Your line was the thread holds. Whose name did you write down? Day one thousand two.

A paper calendar on a kitchen wall, birthdays circled in pen: Grandma, a cousin, the neighbor's twins. Nobody needs a reason to keep them. People are remembered on their day because they belong to someone. Now a different calendar, the kind churches keep. Square after square, a name: Agnes, Benedict, Mary Magdalene, Nicholas. And here's the twist. By old custom, the date beside a saint's name is often not the day they were born. It's the day they died. Today a new block begins, a year of feasts and saints' days, and it starts with the question: why keep them at all?

Start with the word saint. In Paul's letters it doesn't mean a few famous holy people. He writes "to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi": the whole congregation, whoever they were. Saints, in that letter, are simply God's people. Then Christians began remembering particular ones. An early account tells of Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, put to death for his faith. Afterward, his church wrote that they gathered his bones and laid them to rest, and that they meant to meet there with joy and keep the day of his martyrdom as a birthday: to remember those who had finished the race, and to train those still running. A birthday into heaven. Tradition gave it a Latin name, dies natalis. Some find the reason in a line from Hebrews: "Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow". Remember, and follow. And a psalm says: "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints." Churches keep these days differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep full calendars, celebrate the saints at the liturgy, and ask them to pray for the living, the way you'd ask a friend. Anglicans and Lutherans keep calendars of saints and commemorations too, with their own emphases. Some other Protestant churches keep no saints' days, honoring faithful people in sermons and stories and directing every prayer to God alone. Each reads the same Hebrews line. This block walks through the year's feasts and those names, one day at a time.

Here's the practice: keep someone's day, quietly. Settle, and breathe. Hebrews says remember them who have spoken unto you the word. So stay close to home this time: someone who passed something good on to you. A grandparent who said grace, a teacher, a neighbor, someone you've lost. Picture their face, their hands, one thing they did that was good. Let it be their day for a moment. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them. If you don't, simply remember them with care. After the bell, look up whose day it is today on a church calendar, and read a few lines about them. The bell holds the time.
Dies natalis. Latin for birthday, the church's old name for a saint's day of death, the day their life began in heaven.
Your line: a birthday into heaven. Today, find out whose day it is, read three sentences about them, and carry the name with you. Day one thousand two.

1003.title: Advent: the prophets' candle
1003.hook: the first candle recalls the prophets who hoped
1003.howItsDone: In churches that keep Advent, a wreath of greenery holds candles, and one more is lit each Sunday of the season, often with a Bible reading such as Isaiah 9 and a prayer; families also keep wreaths at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dies natalis, and a calendar full of names. Your line was a birthday into heaven. Whose day was it? Day one thousand three.

"The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light." Somebody reads that line in a dim church, or at a kitchen table after supper, and then strikes a match. In front of them is a ring of greenery with candles set in it. Only one gets lit. The others wait their turn, one more each Sunday, until the waiting is over. It's a small flame for such a big sentence. And that's the point. For churches that keep this calendar, the year begins here, with a season called Advent, and a candle for people who hoped.

Advent is the church's word for a coming. It names the weeks before Christmas, when Christians remember the waiting for Christ's birth and, they say, wait again for him to come at the end of time. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others keep it with readings and candles; Orthodox Christians keep their own season of fasting before the Nativity; some churches don't mark it at all. Then the candle. Churches name it differently. Some call the first candle the prophets' candle. Others call it the candle of hope. It comes to the same place. The prophets were people who hoped for what they could not see. Isaiah spoke to a land that knew war and fear, and promised: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined." A few verses on: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given." Christians read that child as Christ; Isaiah himself does not live to see him. Later, Matthew's Gospel tells of Jesus beginning to preach in Galilee, and reaches back for the same words: "The people which sat in darkness saw great light." Jews read Isaiah's promise in their own way, and that reading is theirs to tell. For Christians, the first candle stands for all that waiting. Paul puts the hard truth of it plainly: "hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?" Hope lives in the dark, or it isn't hope. One flame, and the rest still unlit.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one candle. If you have one, light it now. If you don't, turn the room lights down and use any small light you have. Settle, and breathe. Read the line out loud, slowly: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. Then just watch the flame. Let something you are waiting for come to mind, something not yet here. Don't push it to arrive. Let it sit beside the flame. If you pray, you can pray Isaiah's line back to God. If you don't, simply keep watching the light. The bell holds the time.
Advent. The weeks of waiting before Christmas, for a coming. Its first candle, in some churches, remembers the prophets who hoped for a light they did not see.
Your line: hope. Today, notice one small light in a dark place, a window at night, a streetlamp, a kindness nobody had to do, and let it be your first candle. Day one thousand three.

1004.title: Advent: John in the wilderness
1004.hook: the second Sunday: prepare the way
1004.howItsDone: In churches that keep Advent, the second Sunday's readings often tell of John the Baptist and his call to prepare the way of the Lord, and the second candle on the wreath is lit; some Christians make a confession or examine their lives before Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Advent's first candle, for the prophets. Your line was hope. Which small light did you notice in a dark place? Day one thousand four.

A man in a coat of camel's hair, a leather belt around his waist, stands in the river Jordan and shouts. He eats locusts and wild honey. He lives out in the wilderness. And people come anyway: out of Jerusalem, out of the countryside, down to the water, confessing their sins and being baptized by him. He is not the one they've been waiting for, and he says so. He's the one clearing the road. On the second Sunday of Advent, churches that keep the season light a second candle, and his voice comes back.

Mark's Gospel opens with him, and with an old line from the prophets: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." The picture is road-building. Luke spells it out: "Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth". Before someone great arrives, you fill the potholes. You take the boulders off the road. So Advent's second week is about clearing. But clearing what? Luke tells us what happened when the crowds asked John that question. "What shall we do then?" His answers are surprisingly ordinary. To everyone: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise." To the tax collectors: "Exact no more than that which is appointed you." To the soldiers: "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell the tax collectors to quit, or the soldiers to run off into the desert with him. Do your job, honestly. Share what you have. That's the road. Christians differ on how John's call to repent is lived: some through confession to a priest before Christmas, some through quiet self-examination, some through a renewed promise at the altar. Each of these points the same way John did, away from himself. The road isn't for John. It's for the one coming after him.

Here's the practice: find one boulder in the road. Settle, and breathe. Ask John's crowd's question of your own life: what shall I do then? Let one thing come up that's in the way. A grudge. A pile of unopened mail. A habit that keeps tripping someone you love. An extra coat in the closet. Don't solve everything. Just see that one thing clearly, and decide on one small move to clear it. If you pray, you can pray the line from Mark: prepare ye the way of the Lord. If you don't, just hold the picture of an open road. The bell holds the time.
Advent. The weeks of waiting before Christmas. Its second Sunday brings John in the wilderness, crying prepare ye the way of the Lord.
Your line: prepare the way. Today, clear one thing out of someone's path: a chore they dread, a reply they're waiting for, a coat you don't need. Day one thousand four.

1005.title: Gaudete
1005.hook: the third Sunday of Advent is rose-colored: rejoice, the Lord is near
1005.howItsDone: On the third Sunday of Advent, Catholic and some Anglican and Lutheran churches use rose-colored vestments and light a rose candle on the Advent wreath, often hearing Philippians 4:4–7; other churches light a pink candle of joy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John in the wilderness, with camel's hair and a road to clear. Your line was prepare the way. What did you clear out of someone's path? Day one thousand five.

Rose. Not purple. Partway through a season of waiting, of violet cloth and serious readings, the priest in some churches walks out on the third Sunday wearing pink. On the wreath, the candles from earlier Sundays are already burnt down a little, and now a rose-colored one is lit beside them. It looks almost like a mistake. It isn't. The Sunday has a name, and the name is a single Latin word, an order and an invitation at once. Today: Gaudete.

Gaudete means rejoice. It is the first word of the old Latin chant sung as the Mass begins on this Sunday, and the chant is taken from Paul's letter to the Philippians. In the King James Bible: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." Then, a line later, the reason: "The Lord is at hand." Near. Close enough to touch. Now here's what makes the line hard to dismiss as cheerful talk. Paul writes this letter in chains. Earlier in it he mentions "my bonds in Christ", and he isn't sure whether he'll live or die. A prisoner, telling free people to rejoice, twice. So Gaudete Sunday isn't a party thrown because the waiting is over. It's a lighter color in the middle of the waiting, because what's coming is nearer than it was. Tradition says the rose is purple brightened, joy breaking into the fast. Churches keep the day differently. Catholics, and some Anglicans and Lutherans, may wear rose vestments and keep the Latin name. Other churches simply light a pink candle on the wreath, sometimes calling it the candle of joy. Others keep blue or purple all the way through. And Paul goes on, right after the line about the Lord being near: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Careful there means anxious. Paul's point: don't be eaten up by worry; bring it to God, with thanks. That's Gaudete's kind of joy: not pretending the chains aren't there, but rejoicing because someone is near.
screen: `GAUDETE: THE FIRST WORD OF THE CHANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice in one thing. Settle, and breathe. Let one good thing come to mind, small and specific. The way the light hit the kitchen this morning. A message from a friend. A meal. Don't measure it against your worries; let the worries wait outside for two minutes. Just hold the good thing and let yourself be glad of it. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for it, with Paul's line: rejoice in the Lord alway. If you don't, simply stay with the gladness. The bell holds the time.
Gaudete. Latin for rejoice: the name of Advent's third Sunday, rose-colored, from Paul's words, rejoice in the Lord alway, the Lord is at hand.
Your line: rejoice, he is near. Today, the next time someone asks how you are, name one thing you're glad of, and don't follow it with a but. Day one thousand five.

1006.title: Advent: Mary's candle
1006.hook: the fourth Sunday remembers Mary's yes
1006.howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Advent, churches that keep the season light the last candle on the wreath and often read Luke's account of the angel's visit to Mary; Catholics and Orthodox also pray the Hail Mary or other prayers that honor her.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gaudete, the rose Sunday, from a letter written in chains. Your line was rejoice, he is near. What gladness did you name when someone asked? Day one thousand six.

An angel comes in to a young woman in Nazareth. Luke doesn't describe the room. He gives names instead: the angel is Gabriel, the young woman is Mary, and she is promised in marriage to a man called Joseph. The angel's greeting troubles her. What he says next sounds impossible: she will have a son, and his kingdom will have no end. She does not faint. She does not simply nod. She asks a question. And then she gives an answer that is still repeated. On the fourth Sunday of Advent, the last candle before Christmas, her answer comes back. Today: Mary's candle.

Gabriel's first words, in the King James Bible: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says plainly that "she was troubled at his saying". Then comes the promise of a son, and Mary's reply is honest and practical: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The angel doesn't scold her for asking. He explains, as far as it can be explained, and ends: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." Then Mary answers: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Be it unto me. In the Latin Bible the word is fiat, let it be, and tradition calls this moment her fiat. Look at the shape of it. Troubled. A real question. Then yes, with her eyes open. It isn't a yes because nothing frightened her. It's a yes after the question, in a young woman's mouth, with everything riding on it. Churches honor that yes differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor Mary as the Mother of God and ask her to pray for them; the Hail Mary begins with Gabriel's greeting. Protestant churches, in their own ways, honor her as a model of trusting faith, and direct their prayers to God alone. Some churches call the fourth Advent candle Mary's candle; others name it for love, or for the angels. Whatever the name, Luke's sentence from Nazareth stands near the end of the waiting.
screen: `BE IT UNTO ME: LET IT BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one yes. Settle, and breathe. Look for something good you've been holding at arm's length. A call you keep postponing. A kindness you could offer. A small change you know would be good. First do what Mary did: ask your honest question. How? What will it cost? Let the question be there. Then, when you're ready, quietly say yes to it, even a small yes. If you pray, you can pray Mary's words: be it unto me according to thy word. If you don't, simply say, inside, let it be. The bell holds the time.
Advent. The weeks of waiting before Christmas. Its fourth Sunday, in some churches, remembers Mary's yes: be it unto me according to thy word.
Your line: let it be. Today, say yes to the good thing you found, out loud if you can, and take the first small step before the day ends. Day one thousand six.

1007.title: St Nicholas (6 December)
1007.hook: shoes by the door and small gifts for children
1007.howItsDone: In some countries children put out shoes or stockings on the eve of St Nicholas's day and find small gifts in the morning; Orthodox and Catholic churches keep his feast with prayers and hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary's candle on the last Sunday of Advent, and her answer to the angel. Your line was let it be. What good thing did you say yes to? Day one thousand seven.

A pair of small shoes sits by the front door, left out overnight on purpose. In the morning there's something tucked inside: an orange, a few chocolate coins wrapped in gold foil, maybe a little toy. Nobody saw who put them there. That's the point. In parts of Europe, children set out their shoes, or hang a stocking, on the eve of St Nicholas's day, and wake up to find that someone came in the night. The custom is sweet and small, and it hides a serious old story about money, shame, and a window left open in the dark. Today, St Nicholas.

Nicholas was a bishop of Myra, a town on the southern coast of what is now Turkey. Beyond that, much of what people tell about him comes from tradition, and it's honest to say so. The best-known story goes like this. A father in his town has lost everything. He has daughters, and no money for their dowries, so no one will marry them, and the family is facing ruin and disgrace. Nicholas hears about it. He doesn't knock. He doesn't make a speech. At night he comes to the house and tosses a bag of gold through the window, and slips away. The story says he came back again, so the father hid and watched, and finally caught him. And Nicholas asked him to tell no one. Why the secrecy? The story is acting out a saying of Jesus from the Sermon on the Mount. In the King James Bible: "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly." Giving in secret protects the one who receives. The father doesn't have to say thank you to a rich man in the street. He doesn't owe anyone. And it protects the giver too, from the small pleasure of being seen being good. Orthodox, Catholic and some other churches keep Nicholas's day as a feast. Even people who keep no saints' days may know a version of him, because some trace the gift-bringer of Christmas, the one called Santa Claus, back to this bishop and his bags of gold. Underneath the red suit is a man throwing money through a window and running away.

Here's the practice: plan one small gift that no one will trace back to you. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind: a neighbor, a coworker, a person at the bus stop, someone who has had a hard week. Then choose the gift. Coins left where a child will find them. A paid-for coffee. A note with no name on it. A bill quietly covered. Keep it small, and keep it secret. If you pray, you can hold that person before God for a moment. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and decide when you'll leave it. The bell holds the time.
St Nicholas. A bishop of Myra, remembered for gifts given at night through a window, and for asking that nobody be told.
Your line: give in secret. Today, leave your small gift where it will be found, and walk away before anyone asks who left it. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: St Lucy (13 December)
1008.hook: in Sweden, girls in white with candle crowns bring light in the darkest weeks
1008.howItsDone: In Sweden and other Nordic countries, Lucia processions are held in homes, schools and churches, led by a girl in white with a crown of candles; Catholic and Orthodox churches also keep her day as a martyr's feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Nicholas, the bishop who threw gold through a window and ran. Your line was give in secret. Did your small gift get left, and did anyone catch you? Day one thousand eight.

It's still pitch black outside. In a Swedish house, a door opens and a girl walks in wearing a long white gown with a red sash, and on her head a crown of greenery with candles burning in it. She carries a tray of coffee and saffron buns, and she's singing. Behind her, sometimes, come brothers and sisters in white, holding candles of their own. In schools, churches and town squares across Sweden, the same scene plays out on the same morning, in weeks when the northern sun barely shows itself. The girl is playing a part. The part is a young woman from Sicily, a long way south. Today, St Lucy.

Lucy lived in Syracuse, on the island of Sicily, when Christians there could be put to death for their faith. Tradition remembers her as a young woman who gave away what had been saved for her marriage to feed the poor, and who died a martyr rather than give up her faith. Beyond that, the stories grew in the telling. One story people tell in the north says Lucy brought food to Christians hiding underground, and wore candles on her head so both hands were free to carry it. It's a story, not history, but it explains the crown. Why would Sweden, a country long shaped by the Lutheran church and far from Sicily, keep the day of an early martyr at all? Partly because of when it falls. Mid-December in the north is the deep end of the dark. A girl walking in with light on her head, in the blackest hour of the morning, says something without a word. The Gospel of John says it in words. In the King James Bible: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." Some readers hear understood in that word comprehended; others hear overcame, as if the darkness tried to grasp the light and put it out. Either way, the light is still shining. And Jesus hands that light to ordinary people in the Sermon on the Mount: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." That's what the saints' days of this week have been about: real people, a bishop with a bag of gold, a girl with bread for the poor, who carried a little light into a dark place.

Here's the practice: bring light to a dark room. Start in the dark: step into a room that's dim and stand there a moment before anything is lit. Then carry in one thing: a candle, if it's safe, or a small lamp, or even your phone screen turned low. Set it down in the middle of the room. Notice how far one small light reaches, how the corners stay dark and the middle doesn't. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say the words from John: the light shineth in darkness. If you don't, just watch the light and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
St Lucy. A young martyr of Syracuse, remembered for feeding the poor, and in Sweden by girls in white with a crown of candles in the dark of December.

Your line: light in the dark. This week began with why we keep saints' days, lit the Advent candles one by one, and met Nicholas and Lucy. Today, carry one small light into someone's dim afternoon. Day one thousand eight.

some readers hear "overcame" in John 1:5's "comprehended"
some hear understood, others overcame: the darkness couldn't put the light out.

fork.setup: you're Lucy, a young Christian in Syracuse. money has been set aside for your marriage. what do you do with it?
options: keep it safe for the wedding.
give it away to feed the poor.
hide it until the persecution is over.
fork.reveal: tradition remembers her giving it to the poor — and that is part of why she is honored as a saint.

original.note: Greek: light — the word in John 1:5, "the light shineth in darkness."

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty Swedish Christmas custom.
what it means: the feast of Lucy, a martyr of Syracuse remembered for feeding the poor.
what a scholar hears: John 1:5 read two ways — the darkness did not understand the light, or could not overcome it.
